title: Versailles from Paris: which train, Palace ticket or Passport, and what fits in half a day
subtitle: Three railway lines, three kinds of ticket, and an estate too large for a morning. How to choose.
excerpt: How to reach the Palace of Versailles from Paris by train, what separates the Palace ticket from the Passport, why the gardens decide the matter, and a half-day route through the palace and down to the Grand Canal.

meta_title: Versailles from Paris: train, Palace ticket or Passport
meta_description: Which train to take to Versailles, what the Palace ticket and the Passport include, when the gardens are free, and what fits in half a day.

featured_image.alt: The Marble Court of the Palace of Versailles, with its black and white paving and gilded balconies

content_html:
[place attraction="palace-of-versailles" city="versailles"]

On the morning of 6 October 1789 a crowd that had walked out from Paris the day before, led by the market women of the city, broke into the palace of Versailles. By the afternoon the king, the queen and their children were in a carriage on the road to Paris, with the crowd around them. The court had lived here since 1682, when Louis XIV moved his government out of the capital. It never came back.

The furniture was auctioned during the Revolution and the building stood half empty for decades. In 1837 King Louis-Philippe reopened it as a museum dedicated "to all the glories of France", and it has been one ever since. The journey that crowd made on foot now takes about forty minutes by train, and the questions are smaller: which train, which ticket, and how much of the estate fits in half a day.

Which train from Paris

Three lines run to three different stations in Versailles:

  • RER C to Versailles Château Rive Gauche. The closest station, ten minutes on foot from the gates. The trains follow the left bank through Saint-Michel Notre-Dame, Musée d'Orsay, Invalides and Champ de Mars Tour Eiffel, and take 35 to 40 minutes. The line has several branches: board only a train whose last stop is Versailles Château Rive Gauche.
  • Line N from Gare Montparnasse to Versailles Chantiers. The quickest ride, under half an hour, followed by about twenty minutes on foot.
  • Line L from Gare Saint-Lazare to Versailles Rive Droite. About thirty-five minutes, then twenty minutes on foot through the town.

In most summers the central section of the RER C is closed for several weeks of track works. If that falls during your stay, use Montparnasse or Saint-Lazare. Buy the return ticket before you leave Paris.

Palace ticket or Passport

The estate has three parts, and the tickets follow them.

  • The Palace ticket is entry to the palace at a booked time: the State Apartments, the Hall of Mirrors, the rooms of the king and the queen.
  • The Passport is the palace at a booked time, plus the estate of Trianon (the Grand Trianon, the Petit Trianon and the Queen's Hamlet) and the gardens on the days when they are charged for.
  • The Trianon ticket covers that estate alone, which opens at noon.

What decides between them is the gardens. On ordinary days they are free. On the days of the Musical Fountains Shows and the Musical Gardens, which fill much of the calendar from spring to the end of October, they need a ticket, and the Palace ticket does not include it. The Passport does. The park beyond the gardens, with the Grand Canal, is free to walkers all year.

A time slot is compulsory for the palace, also for those who enter free, such as visitors under 18 and residents of the European Union under 26: they book a free slot. The palace is closed on Mondays.

So for half a day on an ordinary day, the Palace ticket is enough. The Passport earns its place when you stay the whole day, or on a fountain day.

At the gate

With a timed ticket you use the entrance for individual visitors, on the left side of the main courtyard. A line forms there too, because everybody passes a security check, so arrive a quarter of an hour before your slot. Suitcases and large bags are not let in.

Half a day, in order

The palace, about ninety minutes

The visit runs one way. You look into the Royal Chapel, finished in 1710, from its doorway, then walk the State Apartments, a row of rooms named after gods and planets, to the Hall of Mirrors: 73 metres long, with seventeen windows facing seventeen arches set with 357 mirrors. The German Empire was proclaimed in this room in January 1871, and the Treaty of Versailles was signed in it on 28 June 1919.

The Hall of Mirrors without its crowd: the windows on one side, the arches of mirror on the other. Photo: Myrabella, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

Behind the mirrors is the King's Bedchamber, placed at the exact centre of the building and facing the rising sun. Louis XIV died in it on 1 September 1715. The queen's rooms follow, with the small door beside the bed through which Marie-Antoinette fled on the morning the crowd came in.

The King's Bedchamber, at the centre of the palace, with the balustrade that kept courtiers at a distance. Photo: Zairon, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The gardens, about an hour

André Le Nôtre began laying out the gardens in 1661. From the terrace behind the palace, walk down the steps to the Latona fountain, then along the lawn called the Royal Way to the Apollo fountain and the head of the Grand Canal, which is more than a kilometre and a half long. The fountains play only on show days.

The Latona fountain, below the terrace, and the axis that runs on to the Grand Canal. Photo: Basile Morin, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What does not fit: Trianon

The Grand Trianon, built of pink marble for Louis XIV in 1687, the Petit Trianon, which Louis XVI gave to Marie-Antoinette in 1774, and her hamlet of thatched cottages lie about half an hour on foot from the palace, and they open only at noon. Seeing them as well takes a whole day.

The Queen's Hamlet, at the far end of the estate of Trianon. Photo: Julian Lupyan, via Wikimedia Commons.

Reading the partner's listings

  • The ticket to the palace, the gardens and the estate of Trianon is the full visit: its list of inclusions names the palace, the gardens, Trianon, the Queen's Hamlet and, at weekends, the Coach Gallery. There is no commentary with it.
  • The ticket with an audio tour of the palace and gardens is entry plus a route narrated in the partner's app, on your own phone. Bring earphones, and read the description of the ticket option you pick, because the options differ in what they cover.
  • The Musical Fountains Show ticket is for the gardens on a show day. Its listing carries no list of inclusions: do not assume the palace is part of it.
  • Audio tours marked "without a ticket", of the palace, of the palace and gardens, or of the gardens, are commentary only.

Several of these tickets are sold in separate categories for residents of the European Economic Area and for other visitors. Choose the one that applies to you and carry an identity document.

These are the Versailles tickets and audio tours our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner attraction="palace-of-versailles" match="versailles" limit="6"]

When to go

Tuesdays, the day after the weekly closure, and weekends are the busiest. Wednesday and Thursday are calmer, and the first slot of the morning has the shortest wait. Hours change with the season: the current ones are on our page for the Palace of Versailles.

From here

The market halls of Place du Marché Notre-Dame are ten minutes from the gates, and the King's Kitchen Garden, planted for Louis XIV's table between 1678 and 1683, still grows fruit and vegetables beside the cathedral. If you stay the day, end it in the gardens. See what else there is in Versailles, or open the trip planner for France.

Cover photo: Kimberly Vardeman, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

faqs.q: Which train goes to Versailles from Paris?
faqs.a: The RER C to Versailles Château Rive Gauche stops ten minutes on foot from the palace and takes 35 to 40 minutes from the left bank. Line N from Montparnasse and Line L from Saint-Lazare reach other stations in the town, about twenty minutes on foot from the gates.

faqs.q: Is the Versailles Passport worth it?
faqs.a: It is worth it if you spend the whole day and visit the estate of Trianon, or if you go on a day when the gardens are charged for. For half a day on an ordinary day, the Palace ticket is enough.

faqs.q: Are the gardens of Versailles free?
faqs.a: On ordinary days, yes. On the days of the Musical Fountains Shows and the Musical Gardens, from spring to the end of October, they need a ticket, which the Passport includes and the Palace ticket does not. The park and the Grand Canal are free to walkers all year.

faqs.q: How long do you need at Versailles?
faqs.a: About ninety minutes for the palace and an hour for the gardens down to the Grand Canal, so half a day without the travel. Adding the estate of Trianon makes it a whole day.

faqs.q: Which day is Versailles closed?
faqs.a: The palace is closed on Mondays. Hours change with the season, so check the current ones before you go.

title: Mont-Saint-Michel from Paris in a day: train or coach, and what you have time for
subtitle: Eight hours of travel for four hours on the rock. How the day works, and how to spend the four hours.
excerpt: How to visit Mont-Saint-Michel from Paris in one day: the train through Rennes, the coach tours, the shuttle from the car parks, what is free on the mount and what needs a ticket, and a plan for the hours you have.
longtail_phrases: can you do Mont-Saint-Michel as a day trip from Paris
how to get to Mont-Saint-Michel from Paris by train
is Mont-Saint-Michel free to enter
how many steps to the abbey of Mont-Saint-Michel
how long do you need at Mont-Saint-Michel
meta_title: Mont-Saint-Michel from Paris in a day: train or coach
meta_description: A day trip to Mont-Saint-Michel from Paris: the train through Rennes, the coach tours, the shuttle, what is free, and a plan for four hours on the mount.

featured_image.alt: Mont-Saint-Michel seen across the salt meadows, with sheep grazing in the foreground

content_html:
[place attraction="mont-saint-michel-abbey" city="paris"]

The story the monks told begins in the year 708. Aubert, bishop of Avranches, dreamed that the archangel Michael ordered him to build a sanctuary on a rock in the bay. He took it for a dream and did nothing. The archangel came a second time, then a third, and the third time pressed a finger into the bishop's forehead. A skull with a hole in it, said to be Aubert's, is still kept in a church in Avranches.

Benedictine monks settled on the rock in 966 and spent the next five centuries building upwards, because there was nowhere else to build. During the Hundred Years' War the English held all of Normandy except this one place, which they besieged for years and never took. After the Revolution it was a prison, until 1863. It stands about 360 kilometres from Paris, which is the whole difficulty of seeing it in a day.

Is a day trip from Paris realistic?

Yes, with open eyes. Whichever way you travel, count on about four hours each way, door to gate. That leaves around four hours on the mount, which is enough for the abbey, the ramparts and the village street, and not enough for a slow lunch or a walk on the sands. If you can give it a night nearby, do. If you cannot, the day works, and the rest of this page is about making those four hours count.

By train: through Rennes

A high-speed train from Paris Montparnasse reaches Rennes in about an hour and a half. From the bus station beside Rennes railway station, a regional coach runs to Mont-Saint-Michel in a little over an hour. The coaches are few and are timed to meet particular trains, so plan the pair together, outward and return, before you buy anything.

This way you are free on the mount, and you need only an abbey ticket. The risk is the connection: if the train is late, the next coach may be hours away.

By coach from Paris

Day tours leave Paris early in the morning and return in the evening, with four hours or more on the road each way and a stop on the motorway. They come in two kinds:

  • Transport with admission. A seat on the coach and a ticket to the abbey. On the mount you are on your own.
  • A guided day tour. The same, with a guide who talks on the coach and walks you through the village on arrival, then leaves you free time.

Read what each one states about the abbey ticket, the guide and the hours on site. The partner's listings for these tours give no list of inclusions, only a description.

These are the day trips to Mont-Saint-Michel from Paris our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner q="mont saint michel paris" match="michel" limit="6"]

If you go by train instead, what you need is the abbey ticket alone. The partner also lists it with an audio tour in its app, and sells the same audio tour without a ticket.

The last three kilometres

No vehicle drives to the gate. Cars and coaches stop at the car parks on the mainland, about two and a half kilometres from the mount. From there free shuttle buses cross in around twelve minutes and set you down a few hundred metres short of the walls. Or you walk, in about forty minutes, with the rock growing in front of you the whole way.

The bridge you cross opened in 2014. It replaced a solid causeway of 1879 that had let the bay silt up, and since then the sea surrounds the mount again at the highest tides of the year.

What is free and what is not

The mount itself is a village, and entering it costs nothing: the gate, the Grande Rue, the ramparts and the parish church are open to all. The ticket is for the abbey at the top, which is a national monument. Visitors under 18 and residents of the European Union under 26 enter the abbey free.

The Grande Rue, the one street of the village, on its way up to the abbey. Photo: Zairon, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Four hours on the mount

  • Go up by the ramparts. Just inside the gates, steps on the right lead onto the wall walk. It climbs to the abbey with the bay on one side and the roofs on the other, and it is far emptier than the street. From the gate to the abbey door there are about 350 steps, whichever way you choose.
  • The abbey, an hour to an hour and a half. The visit starts on the west terrace, with the widest view of the bay, and enters the church: a Romanesque nave of the eleventh century and a Gothic choir, rebuilt after the first one collapsed in 1421.
  • The Marvel. That is the name the monks gave the three-storey building on the north side, put up between 1211 and 1228. You walk it from the top down: the cloister, hung between sky and sea, the refectory, the Guests' Hall, the Knights' Hall.
  • The great wheel. In the prison years, inmates walked inside a wooden wheel to haul supplies up the rock on a sledge. It is still in place.
  • Come down by the Grande Rue. One steep street of stone houses, now shops and restaurants. On a day trip, a sandwich on the ramparts is a better use of time than a table.

The cloister, on the top level of the building the monks called the Marvel. Photo: Benh Lieu Song, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

On the tip of the spire stands a gilded archangel by the sculptor Emmanuel Frémiet, set there in 1897.

The tides

The bay has some of the largest tides in Europe: at their strongest, the difference between low and high water is around fourteen metres, and the sea draws back for kilometres. That is the view from the ramparts at low tide. Do not walk out onto the sands on your own. There is quicksand, and the water returns faster than a person walks. Crossings of the bay are made with licensed guides, and they do not fit a day trip from Paris.

Low tide seen from the ramparts: the sea has drawn back out of sight. Photo: DimiTalen, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

Hours of the abbey change with the season: see our page for the Abbey of Mont-Saint-Michel.

From here

If the day convinces you to stay longer in the west, Rennes, where the train stops, has a medieval quarter of timber-framed houses a short walk from the station, and the walled port of Saint-Malo is on the same coast. Before you leave the mount, the ramparts are worth a second walk when the light drops. For the rest of the country, open the trip planner for France or the attractions map.

Cover photo: Eric Kilby, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Can you do Mont-Saint-Michel as a day trip from Paris?
faqs.a: Yes, as a long day. Count on about four hours each way by train and coach or by tour coach, which leaves around four hours on the mount: enough for the abbey, the ramparts and the village street.

faqs.q: How do you get to Mont-Saint-Michel from Paris by train?
faqs.a: Take a high-speed train from Paris Montparnasse to Rennes, about an hour and a half, then the regional coach from the bus station beside Rennes station, a little over an hour. The coaches are few, so plan the connection both ways.

faqs.q: Is Mont-Saint-Michel free to enter?
faqs.a: The village, the main street and the ramparts are free. The abbey at the top needs a ticket, except for visitors under 18 and residents of the European Union under 26.

faqs.q: How many steps are there to the abbey of Mont-Saint-Michel?
faqs.a: About 350 from the gate of the village to the door of the abbey, by the street or by the ramparts. There is no lift.

faqs.q: Can you walk on the sand around Mont-Saint-Michel?
faqs.a: Not on your own. The bay has quicksand and a tide that comes in faster than a person walks. Crossings are made with licensed guides.

title: Sainte-Chapelle: how the timed entry and the security line work, and whether to add the Conciergerie
subtitle: A chapel inside a courthouse, a ticket for a time that is not quite the time you get in, and a second monument next door.
excerpt: Why the line at the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris is slow even with a ticket, how the timed entry really works, how to read the windows once inside, and whether the combined ticket with the Conciergerie is worth it.
longtail_phrases: how long is the line at Sainte-Chapelle with a ticket
does a Sainte-Chapelle ticket skip the security line
is the Conciergerie worth visiting
what time of day is best for Sainte-Chapelle
how long does Sainte-Chapelle take
meta_title: Sainte-Chapelle: timed entry, security line, Conciergerie
meta_description: Why the Sainte-Chapelle line is slow even with a ticket, how the timed entry works, how to read the windows, and whether to add the Conciergerie.

featured_image.alt: The tall stained glass windows of the apse in the upper chapel of the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris

content_html:
[place attraction="sainte-chapelle" city="paris"]

In 1239 King Louis IX of France bought the Crown of Thorns. Its owner, the emperor Baldwin II of Constantinople, was short of money and had pledged it to Venetian merchants, so the king paid off the debt: 135,000 livres, a large share of what the crown of France earned in a year. When the relic arrived, Louis carried it into Paris barefoot.

Then he built a box for it. The chapel in the courtyard of his palace went up in about seven years and was consecrated on 26 April 1248. It cost some 40,000 livres, less than a third of what it was made to hold. The relic left during the Revolution and is now kept at Notre-Dame. The box remains, and so does the palace around it, which became the law courts of Paris. That is why visiting a chapel here starts like boarding a flight.

Why the line is slow

The Sainte-Chapelle stands inside the Palais de Justice, a working courthouse. Every visitor enters from the boulevard du Palais through a security post with scanners, a few people at a time. On the pavement there are usually two lines, one for people with a ticket and one for people without, and both end at that same post.

So "skip the line" here means the shorter of two lines. Nobody skips the check. Pocket knives, scissors and other sharp objects are not let through, and there is no cloakroom for them or for a suitcase. Come with a small bag.

How the timed entry works

  • The ticket is for a slot. You choose a time when you book. The popular hours sell out in season, and the monument is small, so few people are let in at once.
  • The slot is when you join the line, not when you enter. On a quiet morning you are inside in ten minutes. On a busy afternoon the check can add half an hour or more.
  • Do not come very early. Ten to fifteen minutes before the time on the ticket is right.
  • Free admission still needs a slot. Visitors under 18 and residents of the European Union under 26 enter free, and book a time like everyone else.

The first slot of the day has the shortest wait. For the glass, though, weather matters more than the hour: on a grey day the windows are dim, on a bright one they burn. Morning sun lights the apse, and late afternoon lights the rose window at the other end.

Inside: half an hour, two chapels

The lower chapel

You enter at ground level, into a low hall that served the people of the palace household. Its vault is painted blue and gold. Most visitors cross it quickly, and they are right to: the reason for the building is upstairs, at the top of a narrow spiral staircase.

The vault of the lower chapel. The paint is a restoration of the nineteenth century. Photo: Guilhem Vellut, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

The upper chapel

The king's chapel, level with his apartments, has almost no walls. Fifteen windows, each about fifteen metres high, stand between thin piers of stone, and hold 1,113 scenes. Around two thirds of the glass is the original of the thirteenth century.

The windows are a book with an order. Begin on the left as you come in, with Genesis, and move along the north side and round the apse, reading each window from the bottom upwards. The Passion is in the centre of the apse, above the platform where the relics were shown. The last window on the south side, beside the door, tells the story you read above: the Crown of Thorns arriving in Paris, with the king carrying it.

The rose window on the west wall is later, of the end of the fifteenth century, and shows the Apocalypse.

The rose window of the west wall, two centuries younger than the rest of the glass. Photo: Gerda Arendt, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

Should you add the Conciergerie?

Two minutes along the same boulevard is the other surviving part of the medieval palace. A combined ticket covers both, and there is rarely a wait at the second door.

What it holds: the Hall of the Men-at-Arms, built under King Philip the Fair in the first years of the fourteenth century, 64 metres long, among the largest medieval halls left in Europe. Beyond it are the rooms of the prison this became. In 1793 and 1794 the Revolutionary Tribunal sat upstairs, and those it condemned waited here. Marie-Antoinette was held in a cell from 2 August to 16 October 1793. The cell itself was turned into a memorial chapel in 1815.

The Hall of the Men-at-Arms in the Conciergerie, built in the first years of the fourteenth century. Photo: Chatsam, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

Add it if the Revolution interests you and you have an hour. The rooms are large and mostly bare, and their story is told on panels and a tablet guide. If your time is short, skip it and look at the towers from the quay instead, which is free.

The Conciergerie from across the Seine. The towers can be seen without a ticket. Photo: Dietmar Rabich, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

With a combined ticket you still book a time for the Sainte-Chapelle. Do the chapel first, at your slot, and the Conciergerie afterwards.

Reading the partner's listings

  • The Sainte-Chapelle ticket with an audio tour is entry for a time slot plus commentary in the partner's app on your own phone. Bring earphones.
  • The Conciergerie and Sainte-Chapelle ticket with an audio tour is the combined entry, with a narrated route through both.
  • The audio tour marked "without a ticket" is the commentary alone. You book your entry separately.

The tickets come in two categories, for residents of the European Economic Area and for other visitors. Pick the one that applies and carry an identity document.

These are the Sainte-Chapelle tickets and audio tours our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner q="la sainte-chapelle" match="chapelle" limit="3"]

Hours change through the year, and the courthouse can alter access at short notice: see our page for the Sainte-Chapelle.

From here

You are in the middle of the island where Paris began. Notre-Dame, reopened in December 2024 after the fire, is five minutes to the east. In the other direction, Place Dauphine is a quiet triangle of old houses behind the courthouse, and it leads to the Pont Neuf, finished in 1607 and the oldest bridge still standing in the city. See the rest of the Palais de la Cité, what else there is in Paris, or open the trip planner for France.

Cover photo: Gerda Arendt, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

faqs.q: Does a Sainte-Chapelle ticket skip the security line?
faqs.a: No. A ticket puts you in the line for ticket holders, which is shorter than the line for people without one, but everybody passes the same security check at the entrance of the courthouse.

faqs.q: How long is the wait at Sainte-Chapelle with a timed ticket?
faqs.a: About ten minutes in the first slot of a quiet morning, and half an hour or more on a busy afternoon. The time on the ticket is when you join the line, not when you walk in.

faqs.q: How long does a visit to Sainte-Chapelle take?
faqs.a: Thirty to forty-five minutes for the two chapels. Add about an hour if you also visit the Conciergerie with a combined ticket.

faqs.q: Is the Conciergerie worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes if the French Revolution interests you: it has a great medieval hall and the prison rooms where Marie-Antoinette was held in 1793. The rooms are mostly bare, so skip it if your time is short.

faqs.q: What time of day is best for Sainte-Chapelle?
faqs.a: The first slot of the morning has the shortest wait. For the glass, a sunny day matters more than the hour: morning light is on the apse, late afternoon light on the rose window.

title: Musée Rodin in ninety minutes: where The Thinker, The Kiss and The Gates of Hell are
subtitle: Half of this museum is a garden. Which works are outdoors, which are in the house, and what the tickets include.
excerpt: A ninety-minute route through the Musée Rodin in Paris: the bronzes in the garden, the marbles in the house, the room of Camille Claudel, whether the famous works are the originals, and what each ticket includes.
secondary_keywords: where is The Thinker in Paris
longtail_phrases: what to see at the Musée Rodin
how long does the Rodin Museum take
is The Thinker at the Rodin Museum the original
where is The Kiss by Rodin
which day is the Rodin Museum closed
meta_title: Musée Rodin in ninety minutes: what to see, and tickets
meta_description: Where The Thinker, The Kiss and The Gates of Hell are in the Musée Rodin, a ninety-minute route through garden and house, and what the tickets include.

featured_image.alt: The Hôtel Biron, home of the Musée Rodin in Paris, seen across the lawn and the pond of its garden

content_html:
[place attraction="musee-rodin" city="paris"]

In 1908 the poet Rainer Maria Rilke, who had been Auguste Rodin's secretary, wrote to tell him about a house. The Hôtel Biron, a mansion of around 1730 on the rue de Varenne, had been a convent school until the nuns were made to leave in 1904. While its fate was decided, rooms in it were let cheaply to artists: Jean Cocteau, Henri Matisse and the dancer Isadora Duncan were among the tenants. The garden had run wild.

Rodin took four rooms on the ground floor and slowly spread through the rest. When the state, which had bought the property, moved to clear the tenants out, he made an offer: all his works, his drawings and his collections, in exchange for the house becoming his museum. Parliament accepted in 1916. He died in November 1917, and the museum opened in 1919. It is still the house and the garden he chose, which is why half of the visit is outdoors.

How the museum is laid out

From the entrance on the rue de Varenne you come first into a rose garden in front of the house. The largest bronzes stand here, among clipped yews. The mansion holds eighteen rooms on two floors, arranged roughly in the order of Rodin's life. Behind it a long lawn runs down to a round pond, with more sculpture along the paths and a café under the trees.

One ticket covers the house, the garden and the temporary exhibition. Ninety minutes are enough for all of it at an easy pace. If the weather is uncertain, do the garden first.

In the garden

The Thinker

He was designed around 1880 as a small figure for the top of a doorway: the poet Dante, looking down on his own Hell. Enlarged in 1904 and cast in bronze, he was paid for by public subscription and set up in front of the Panthéon in 1906. He was moved to this garden in 1922. The gilded dome behind him belongs to the Invalides, next door.

The Thinker in the garden, on the pedestal it has stood on since 1922. Photo: Shadowgate, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

The Gates of Hell

In 1880 the state ordered a bronze door for a museum of decorative arts. The museum was never built, and Rodin worked on the door for the rest of his life, 37 years, without seeing it cast. It carries close to two hundred figures. Look for the first Thinker in the panel above the doors, and for the pair of lovers who later became The Kiss, and who were taken off the door because they looked too happy for the place.

The Gates of Hell, in the rose garden. The small figure above the doors is the first Thinker. Photo: Shadowgate, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

The Burghers of Calais

Six leading men of Calais who, in 1347, walked out to the English king with ropes round their necks to save their town. Rodin wanted them at ground level, among the passers-by, and not on a tall pedestal. Walk round the group: no two faces take it the same way.

The Burghers of Calais: six men walking out of their town in 1347. Photo: Shadowgate, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

Balzac

A writers' society ordered a monument to the novelist and, in 1898, refused the result: a figure wrapped in a dressing gown, all head. Rodin kept the plaster at home. It was cast in bronze only in 1939.

In the house

  • The Age of Bronze. The life-size nude of 1877 that made his name, partly through scandal: it was so true that he was accused of having cast it from a living man.
  • The Kiss. The marble was ordered by the state in 1888. The lovers are Paolo and Francesca, from Dante. Other marble versions are in Copenhagen and London.
  • The Cathedral. Two hands arched towards each other. Look again: they are two right hands.
  • The Walking Man. No head, no arms, and all the movement in the legs.
  • The room of Camille Claudel. Rodin's pupil, collaborator and lover, and a great sculptor in her own right. The Waltz and The Age of Maturity are here.
  • Rodin's own collection. He bought paintings by his friends. Van Gogh's portrait of Père Tanguy hangs upstairs, with works by Monet and Renoir.

The Kiss, in marble, inside the house. Photo: Thibsweb, via Wikimedia Commons.

Are these the originals?

It is the question most visitors ask, and the answer depends on the material. A marble is one object. A bronze is cast from a mould, and Rodin's bronzes exist in several casts: there are Thinkers of this size in a number of cities. The museum inherited his plaster models and the right to cast from them, and French law limits the casts that count as originals to twelve. The Thinker in this garden is one of the first, the very one that stood at the Panthéon.

Tickets and the line

The Musée Rodin is not sold by time slot the way the Louvre is, and the wait at the door is usually short: a bag check, then the desk. It is closed on Mondays. Visitors under 18, and residents of the European Union under 26, are admitted free, so do not buy an adult ticket for a child.

What the partner's listings include:

  • The entrance ticket covers the permanent collection, the temporary exhibition and the sculpture garden. No commentary.
  • The ticket with an audio tour adds about an hour of commentary in the partner's app. Bring earphones.
  • The city audio walk with a Rodin Museum ticket includes entry, but its commentary is for a walk through Paris that starts at the museum. Its exclusions say plainly that there is no audio inside.
  • The audio tour "without a ticket" is commentary only.

These are the Rodin Museum tickets and audio tours our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner attraction="musee-rodin" match="rodin" limit="4"]

Practical notes

  • The nearest metro station is Varenne, on line 13, two minutes away. Copies of Rodin's sculptures stand on its platform.
  • Late afternoon gives the bronzes their best light, and the garden empties in the last hour.
  • Large bags go to the cloakroom.

Current hours are on our page for the Musée Rodin.

From here

The Invalides is across the street: the Army Museum and, under the dome you saw from the garden, the tomb of Napoleon. The Musée d'Orsay, which shows a plaster of The Gates of Hell, is a quarter of an hour on foot towards the river. Rodin's other house, at Meudon, where he is buried beneath a Thinker, is a separate museum with limited opening days. For the rest of Paris, open the trip planner for France.

Cover photo: Lennart Kjellman, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

faqs.q: What should you see at the Musée Rodin?
faqs.a: In the garden: The Thinker, The Gates of Hell, The Burghers of Calais and the Balzac. In the house: The Kiss, The Age of Bronze, The Cathedral, The Walking Man and the room of Camille Claudel.

faqs.q: How long does the Musée Rodin take?
faqs.a: About ninety minutes for the garden and the house at an easy pace. An hour is enough if you keep to the best-known works.

faqs.q: Is The Thinker at the Musée Rodin the original?
faqs.a: It is an original bronze cast, enlarged in 1904, and the one that stood in front of the Panthéon from 1906 until it was moved to the garden in 1922. Bronzes are cast in several copies, so other Thinkers exist elsewhere.

faqs.q: Where is The Kiss by Rodin?
faqs.a: The marble ordered by the French state in 1888 is inside the house of the Musée Rodin in Paris. Other marble versions are in Copenhagen and London.

faqs.q: Which day is the Musée Rodin closed?
faqs.a: It is closed on Mondays. Hours can change, so check the current ones before you go.

title: Chambord or Chenonceau: which Loire château to choose, and how to reach them without a car
subtitle: One was built by a king to be looked at, the other by a line of women to be lived in. The train reaches both, differently.

featured_image.alt: The towers, chimneys and lanterns of the Château de Chambord seen from its lawn

content_html:
[place attraction="chateau-de-chambord" city="blois"]

King François I was twenty-five when he ordered a hunting lodge in the forest near Blois, in 1519. What rose there over the next decades has more than four hundred rooms and 282 fireplaces. In a reign of thirty-two years he slept in it for about seventy-two nights. Nobody knows for certain who designed it. Leonardo da Vinci, the king's guest at Amboise, died a few months before the first stone was laid, and the staircase at the centre of the plan has been linked with his name ever since.

Fifty kilometres to the south-west, at about the same time, a tax official named Thomas Bohier was building a house on the piers of an old mill in the river Cher. He was away at the wars, so his wife, Katherine Briçonnet, ran the works. Later a king's mistress added a bridge to it, and a queen put a gallery on the bridge. These are the two châteaux most visitors to the Loire want to see, and unless you have a car and a long day, you have to choose.

Chambord: the building is the visit

Chambord was made to impress from outside, and it does. Inside, the plan is a Greek cross of four great halls around the famous staircase: two spirals wound round the same hollow core, so that a person going up never meets a person coming down, though they glimpse each other through the openings.

The hollow core of the double staircase. Through the openings you see the people on the other flight. Photo: Thesupermat, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The staircase leads to the roof terraces, which are the best part: a small town of chimneys, turrets and dormers, built so the court could watch the hunt come home. Around the château lies a walled park about the size of inner Paris.

The roof of Chambord, where the carving is: dormers, chimneys and turrets at arm’s length. Photo: Fab5669, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The weak point is the rooms. The court travelled with its furniture, the place was never lived in for long, and much of it is bare. Come for architecture and space, and allow two to three hours.

Chenonceau: the house is the visit

Chenonceau is small enough to take in and has been lived in for five centuries. Henri II gave it in 1547 to Diane de Poitiers, who built the bridge over the Cher. When he died in 1559 his widow, Catherine de' Medici, made Diane hand it over, and raised the two-storey gallery, sixty metres long, on top of the bridge. In the eighteenth century Louise Dupin, who held a salon here, was respected enough locally to bring it through the Revolution unharmed.

Chenonceau: the first house on the right, and the gallery that crosses the Cher. Photo: Gzen92, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The gallery has a later story too. In the First World War it was a hospital ward. From 1940 to 1942 the Cher was the line between occupied France and the free zone: the front door of the château was on one side, and the door at the far end of the gallery opened onto the other.

The rooms are furnished and filled with flowers grown on the estate, the kitchens are down inside the piers of the bridge, and two formal gardens, one named for each of the rival women, flank the forecourt. It is also the busier of the two. Allow two hours.

Which one, then

  • Choose Chambord if you care most about architecture, want the roof and the forest, or are travelling with children who need room to run.
  • Choose Chenonceau if you want interiors, gardens and a story with people in it, or if you are coming by train with no wish to depend on a shuttle bus.
  • Both in one day is realistic only by car or on an organised coach tour from Paris. By public transport, give each its own day, or sleep in Blois, Amboise or Tours.

Without a car

To Chenonceau

This is the easy one. A high-speed train from Paris Montparnasse reaches Saint-Pierre-des-Corps, the main-line station of Tours, in about an hour. From Tours a regional train runs to the village station of Chenonceaux in about half an hour, and the ticket office of the château is a five-minute walk from the platform. The regional trains are not frequent, so choose the return before you go.

To Chambord

Trains from Paris Austerlitz reach the station of Blois-Chambord in about an hour and a half. Despite the name, the château is some seventeen kilometres from Blois. From spring to autumn a shuttle bus links the station with Chambord a few times a day. Outside those months, or outside its timetable, the choice is a taxi. Check the shuttle's dates for the year before you count on it.

The tickets, and two more châteaux

The partner's listings for the Loire are plain entry tickets: no transport, no guide, and no list of inclusions beyond a description, so read it. Two points are worth knowing:

  • Chambord is a state monument. Visitors under 18 and residents of the European Union under 26 enter free. The partner's ticket is sold in separate categories for residents of the European Economic Area and for others, and a tablet guide called the HistoPad is an optional extra.
  • Chenonceau is privately owned. The state's free-entry rules do not apply, and it has its own reduced tickets for children and students.

The same list holds two châteaux near Tours. Villandry is visited for its gardens, laid out again in Renaissance style from 1906 by Joachim Carvallo, with a kitchen garden planted like embroidery. Azay-le-Rideau, built between 1518 and 1527 on an island in the river Indre, is the small, perfect one, and it has a railway station of its own, about twenty minutes on foot from the gate. The fortress of Angers, further west, keeps the Apocalypse Tapestry, woven in the 1370s.

The gardens of Villandry, which are the reason to go there. Photo: Thérèse Gaigé, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

These are the château tickets our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner q="château de" match="chambord,chenonceau,villandry,azay" limit="6"]

Opening hours differ from one château to the next and by season: see our pages for the Château de Chambord and the Château de Chenonceau.

From here

If you came for Chambord, the royal château in the middle of Blois is five minutes on foot from the station and shows four centuries of building around one courtyard. If you came for Chenonceau, Amboise is one stop away: the royal château above the Loire, where Leonardo is buried, and the Clos Lucé, the house where he spent his last three years. To place the rest, open the attractions map of France.

Cover photo: Ввласенко, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

faqs.q: Is Chambord or Chenonceau better?
faqs.a: They suit different visitors. Chambord is the larger and the more striking building, with its double staircase, roof terraces and forest, but its rooms are mostly bare. Chenonceau is smaller, furnished, set on a bridge over the river Cher, with gardens.

faqs.q: How do you get to Chenonceau from Paris by train?
faqs.a: Take a high-speed train from Paris Montparnasse to Saint-Pierre-des-Corps, about an hour, then a regional train from Tours to Chenonceaux, about half an hour. The château is a five-minute walk from the station.

faqs.q: How do you get to Chambord without a car?
faqs.a: Take a train from Paris Austerlitz to Blois-Chambord, about an hour and a half. From spring to autumn a shuttle bus runs from the station to the château, some seventeen kilometres away. At other times you need a taxi.

faqs.q: Can you visit Chambord and Chenonceau in one day?
faqs.a: By car or on an organised coach tour from Paris, yes. By public transport it is not realistic: give each château its own day, or stay overnight in Blois, Amboise or Tours.

faqs.q: How long do you need at Chambord?
faqs.a: Two to three hours for the château, the staircase and the roof terraces. Chenonceau takes about two hours with its gardens.
